Walk-in closet Small bedroom or apartment belongings 5×15 75 sq. ft. Large walk-in closet Furniture, appliances, and boxes 10×10 100 sq. ft. About half a one-car garage Contents of multiple rooms 10×15 150 sq. ft. Large bedroom Furniture and belongings from several rooms 10×20 200 sq. ft. About a one-car garage Contents of a three-bedroom home 10×25 250 sq. ft. Larger than a one-car garage Contents of a three- to four-bedroom home 10×30 300 sq. ft. Large household storage space Contents of a four- to five-bedroom home Storage unit dimensions are generally expressed as width by length . Exact dimensions and ceiling heights can vary by New York City facility and individual unit . What Are the Dimensions of a 5×5 Storage Unit in New York City? A 5×5 storage unit offers roughly 25 square feet of space, making it about the size of a large closet . This compact option is great for New York City apartment dwellers who need a bit more room for: Organizing storage boxes Stowing festive holiday gear Tucking away off-season apparel Stashing small furniture pieces Keeping sports gear tidy Storing miscellaneous personal items If you’re in an apartment or condo in spots like the Upper East Side, Williamsburg, Long Island City, Astoria, or Park Slope , a 5×5 unit provides just enough extra storage without committing to an overly large space. What Are the Dimensions of a 5×10 Storage Unit in New York City? A 5×10 storage unit spans around 50 square feet , comparable to the space of a walk-in closet . It’s perfect for holding items like: Bedroom furniture A mattress and bed frame Storage boxes and bins Small appliances Bicycles Seasonal items This unit size is ideal for New York City renters who are transitioning between apartments or need some additional space for bedroom essentials. What Are the Dimensions of a 5×15 Storage Unit in New York City? A 5×10 storage unit spans around 50 square feet , comparable to the space of a walk-in closet . It’s perfect for holding items like: Bedroom furniture Mattress and bed frame Storage bins Small appliances Bicycles Seasonal decorative items This unit size is ideal for New York City renters who are transitioning between apartments or need some additional space for bedroom essentials. What Are the Dimensions of a 10×10 Storage Unit in New York City? A 10×10 storage unit offers around 100 square feet of space, comparable to about half the size of a one-car garage . It’s spacious enough to accommodate: Living room couches and armchairs Complete bedroom furniture sets Mattresses of various sizes Dining tables and chairs Household appliances Numerous boxes and crates This size is ideal for New York City residents who are shifting between apartments or houses, undergoing renovations, or looking to temporarily store belongings from several rooms, all without committing to a larger unit. What Are the Dimensions of a 10×15 Storage Unit in New York City? A 10×10 storage unit offers around 100 square feet of space, comparable to about half the size of a one-car garage . It’s spacious enough to accommodate: Living room couches and armchairs Complete bedroom furniture setups Mattresses of various sizes Dining tables and chairs Essential household appliances Numerous boxes and crates This size is ideal for New York City residents who are shifting between apartments or houses, undergoing renovations, or looking to temporarily store belongings from several rooms, all without committing to a larger unit. What Are the Dimensions of a 10×20 Storage Unit in New York City? Imagine a 10×20 storage unit as having about 200 square feet of space—similar to the area of a one-car garage . This roomy option can comfortably fit the contents of a three-bedroom New York City home , including furniture, appliances, mattresses, and boxes galore. It’s a fantastic choice for those bigger household moves, major renovations, or when you’re in the midst of switching homes and need to stash your stuff somewhere safe and spacious. What Are the Dimensions of a 10×25 Storage Unit in New York City? A 10×25 storage unit measures approximately 10 feet wide by 25 feet long , providing about 250 square feet of floor space. A 10×25 unit may accommodate the contents of a three- to four-bedroom home , depending on the size and number of belongings being stored. It provides room for large furniture, appliances, bedroom sets, dining furniture, boxes, and other household items. For New York City households making a larger move or storing most of a home’s contents during a renovation, the additional five feet of length can provide valuable extra room compared with a 10×20. What Are the Dimensions of a 10×30 Storage Unit in New York City? A 10×30 storage unit measures approximately 10 feet wide by 30 feet long and provides about 300 square feet of floor space. As one of the largest commonly available storage unit sizes, a 10×30 may accommodate belongings from a four- to five-bedroom home , depending on the amount and size of the items. This size can be useful for large New York City household moves, major renovations, or situations where furniture, appliances, boxes, and other belongings need to be stored together. What Should New York City Residents Consider When Choosing a Storage Unit Size? When picking a storage unit in New York City, it’s not just about the size—think about what you’re storing, how long it’ll be there, and how often you’ll need to grab things . Start by measuring your bigger items like couches, mattresses, or dining tables, and figure out how many boxes or storage bins you might need around them. And don’t forget about New York’s seasonal weather ! If your items don’t play nice with temperature changes, humidity, or the winter chill, a climate-controlled unit might be your best bet. Also, consider where the unit is located. Keeping it close to your home, apartment, workplace, or along your usual route can make popping in and out a whole lot easier! What Size Storage Unit Do I Need in New York City? As a general guide: 5×5: Good for boxes, seasonal belongings, and small furniture. 5×10: Useful for a bedroom’s contents or additional apartment storage. 5×15: Provides more room for furniture, appliances, and boxes. 10×10: Can accommodate furniture and belongings from multiple rooms. 10×15: Useful for larger moves and multi-room storage. 10×20: About the footprint of a one-car garage and may hold the contents of a three-bedroom home. 10×25: May accommodate belongings from a three- to four-bedroom home. 10×30: Provides ample space for belongings from a four- to five-bedroom home. These are general estimates. The amount of space you need will depend on the size, number, and arrangement of your belongings. Frequently Asked Questions About Storage Unit Sizes in New York City What is the most common storage unit size in New York City? New York City storage facilities offer a range of sizes, with options commonly including 5×5, 5×10, 5.5×12 6×7.5, 10×10, 10×15, 10×20, 14×5 , and other configurations. Availability varies by facility. How big is a 10×10 storage unit in New York City? A 10×10 storage unit provides approximately 100 square feet of floor space. Its footprint is roughly half the size of a one-car garage and can provide space for furniture, appliances, boxes, and belongings from multiple rooms. What size storage unit do I need for a New York City apartment? If you just need a little extra space for apartment overflow, a 5×5 unit may do the trick. For more furniture, boxes, or seasonal items, a 5×10 or 5×15 gives you a bit more room to work with. If you’re storing belongings from several rooms, a 10×10 may be a better fit. Ultimately, the best unit size depends on how much you have and the size of your larger items. What size storage unit do I need for a one-bedroom New York City home? A 5×10 or 5×15 storage unit may accommodate the contents of a one-bedroom New York City home or apartment, including bedroom furniture, small appliances, boxes, and other household belongings. The right size depends on the amount and size of the items you plan to store. What size storage unit do I need for a two-bedroom New York City home? A 10×10 or 10×15 storage unit can be a great option for storing the belongings from a two-bedroom New York City apartment or home. You’ll typically have room for bedroom and living room furniture, appliances, mattresses, and plenty of boxes. If you have larger pieces of furniture or simply want a little extra breathing room, a 10×15 unit can give you the additional space you need. What size storage unit do I need for a three-bedroom New York City home? A 10×20 storage unit may accommodate the contents of a three-bedroom home, depending on the amount and size of the furniture, appliances, boxes, and other belongings being stored. Should I consider climate-controlled storage in New York City? Climate-controlled storage can be a smart choice if you’re storing items that may be sensitive to changes in temperature or humidity. New York City sees hot, humid summers and cold winters , which can create fluctuating conditions throughout the year. Items such as wooden furniture, electronics, artwork, important documents, clothing, and other delicate belongings may benefit from a more consistent storage environment. If you’re planning to keep your things in storage for several months or longer, it’s worth considering whether climate control is the right fit for what you’re storing.

title: 12 Best Outsource Design Agencies for 2026
summary: Compare the 12 best outsource design agencies across studios, subscriptions and marketplaces, with real pricing and who actually owns the work you pay for.
body_text: Key takeaways: Outsourcing design splits into three models that price and fail differently: studios, subscriptions and talent marketplaces. Picking the wrong one costs more than picking the wrong vendor. Paying for a logo does not make you its owner. Under US copyright law, commissioned design only counts as work made for hire if it falls into one of nine narrow categories, and graphic and web design are not among them. Deloitte found that outsourcing's expected productivity and cost gains are frequently held back by weak governance and contracting rather than by weak suppliers. Ask every candidate who owns the source files, who owns the fonts, and what happens to your work if the contract ends tomorrow. Design gets outsourced for one of two reasons, and they lead to completely different decisions. The first is capacity: you have a design function, it works, and there is more work than people. The second is capability: you have no design function and need one to exist by Thursday. A talent marketplace solves the first badly and the second well. A strategy-led studio does the reverse. Below are twelve providers worth considering, grouped so you can tell which model each one belongs to. We're first, and we have been explicit about where a specialist studio or a marketplace will serve you better than a subscription. The three ways to outsource design Almost every provider in this category is one of three things wearing different marketing. Agencies and studios take a defined project, run discovery, and deliver a finished thing. You get senior strategic thinking and a considered process. You also get statements of work, change orders, and a several-week gap between deciding you need something and someone starting it. Subscriptions and flat-rate services charge monthly for a queue. You submit tasks, they come back, and the price does not change with volume. The tradeoff is that you are buying execution capacity rather than strategic partnership, and a genuinely novel positioning problem is not what the model is built for. Talent marketplaces connect you directly with individual designers, either vetted or open. Buyers searching for outsource web design agencies usually end up here first, because the entry cost looks lowest. You get flexibility and often the lowest cost per hour. You also inherit the management burden: briefing, quality control, continuity and cover when someone disappears. The most common expensive mistake is buying a studio engagement for work that was really a queue, or buying a queue when the actual problem needed a week of strategic thinking first. Our comparison of freelance, in-house and subscription routes goes deeper on where each breaks down. Who owns the design after you pay for it This is the section most outsourcing roundups skip, and it is the one most likely to cost you real money. American buyers tend to assume that paying an external designer makes the company the owner of the result. That assumption is often wrong, and the US Copyright Office is explicit about why. Circular 9 sets out that a work made for hire arises in two ways. Work created by an employee within the scope of employment is automatically work made for hire. Work commissioned from someone who is not your employee is a much narrower case: it qualifies only if it satisfies all four criteria, and the first is that it must fall within one of nine enumerated categories . Those are a contribution to a collective work, part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, a translation, a supplementary work, a compilation, an instructional text, a test, answer material for a test, or an atlas. Read that list again with design work in mind. A logo is not on it. Neither is a brand identity system, a website, an app interface or a set of social templates. It follows that commissioning a logo from a contractor or an overseas studio does not, on its own, make it work made for hire, and the Copyright Office states that where a work is not work made for hire, the individual who created it is the author and the copyright owner. There is one important exception in the other direction. "Part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work" is on the list , so commissioned video and animation can qualify where a logo cannot, provided the parties also "expressly agree in a written instrument signed by them." The practical fix is short. Ask for a written assignment of copyright, signed, covering the specific deliverables, rather than relying on a work-for-hire clause that may not apply to what you are buying. Ask separately about typefaces, because a typeface license covers a specific company and specific uses, and settling the invoice does not move it to you. Deloitte's Global Outsourcing Survey makes the same point from the other end, reporting that the productivity and cost benefits organizations expect from outsourcing are often limited by exactly these governance and contracting weaknesses rather than by supplier quality. The vendor is rarely the problem. The paperwork usually is. The 12 best outsource design agencies The table groups by model first, because that decision comes before vendor choice. Pricing reflects each provider's published rates where they exist. Speed of access varies just as much as price does, and the fastest freelance platforms will put someone on a task in hours where a studio needs weeks. Provider Model Best for Where it's based Pricing (from) Awesomic Subscription Ongoing design across many formats San Francisco, CA $1,490/month ustwo Studio Digital products that need real strategy New York, NY Quote only ParallelHQ Studio UI and UX for SaaS and AI products Austin, TX Quote only Bilberrry Studio Web, app and AI builds end to end Seattle, WA Quote only Gravitate Studio Web design tied to marketing outcomes Vancouver, WA Quote only Toptal Marketplace Senior designers, vetted, fast Remote, US-founded Hourly, varies Near Marketplace Full-time Latin American designers Austin, TX Monthly per hire DesignCrowd Marketplace Crowdsourced concepts and logos Sydney, Australia Per project Draftss Subscription Design plus front-end development Remote Flat monthly DotYeti Subscription Flat-rate design with named designers Dover, DE Flat monthly No Limit Creatives Subscription Graphic and video on one plan Bend, OR Flat monthly Design Buffs Subscription On-brand marketing design at speed Remote Flat monthly Locations come from each provider's own site. Several are deliberately distributed, and where a provider names a headquarters we used it. 1. Awesomic Best for: replacing a hiring cycle you cannot complete or cannot justify. Outsourcing usually gets framed as a cost decision. Often it is really an availability decision, and Kyivstar.Tech is the clearest illustration we have. The Ukrainian technology company hired senior in-house designers twice. Both times those designers were mobilized into the Armed Forces, and each replacement cycle meant four months or more with no creative output at all. Getting headcount approved was a fight; getting budget approved for a service subscription moved quickly. So they stopped trying to hire. What replaced it was not a project engagement. We plugged into their existing Slack and Kanban workflow with no onboarding deck and no project-manager relay, briefs going in and designs coming back the same day. They were matched with Yuriy, a senior designer who has stayed with the account long enough to know the brand properly, delivering first iterations within 24 hours. Every asset still clears Kyivstar's legal and PR review, which is the real test of whether speed came at the cost of quality. That is the shape of the model. You are not buying a project, you are buying continuity that does not depend on one person's employment status. How it works: work goes in as tasks, a screened specialist picks one up within hours, revision rounds are uncapped, and the number of live tasks flexes month to month. Services: brand identity, web and product design, UI/UX, Webflow and Framer build, motion and video, presentations, social and ad creative, copywriting and QA on the higher tier. Pricing: Graphic Pack costs $1,490 monthly, or $1,190 on the quarterly plan with its three-month floor. All-in-One costs $2,995 monthly, or $2,396 quarterly, and adds no-code development, copywriting and QA. Dedicated Talent pairs one full-time specialist with a dedicated PM and is scoped individually. AI Designer is $200 monthly. Proof: 4,000-plus customers, 20,000-plus delivered projects, 4.9 scores on Trustpilot and Google Play, and a talent pool that admits 0.82 percent of applicants. Y Combinator backed. Honest limits: if your problem is a six-week research and positioning exercise before anyone opens a design tool, a studio below is the better buy. Subscriptions are built for continuous output, not for discovery. See how we structure work with agencies if you are an agency looking to white-label capacity. Book demo 2. ustwo Model: studio. ustwo is a digital product studio with a New York office on Jay Street alongside London and Sweden. It works on substantial product problems rather than marketing collateral, and is known as much for its own games and products as for client work. This is a genuine partner engagement, priced accordingly, and worth it when the product question is unresolved rather than the design capacity being short. Services: product strategy, UX and UI design, design systems, product development. Pricing: enterprise project scoping, no public rates. Why buyers shortlist it: it will push back on the brief, which is the thing you are actually paying a studio for. 3. ParallelHQ Model: studio. ParallelHQ positions itself as a UI and UX design agency for AI startups and SaaS companies, operating from Austin with a team in Bengaluru. That structure is common in this category and worth knowing about up front, since it affects both cost and working hours. Its focus on a single product category means it arrives with pattern knowledge rather than learning your category on your budget. Services: UI and UX design, product design, design systems, web design. Pricing: scoped per engagement. Where it fits: early-stage software teams that need product design specifically, not general marketing design. 4. Bilberrry Model: studio. Bilberrry works from 1st Avenue in Seattle as a digital agency covering web, apps and AI work. It sits in the useful middle ground between a boutique design studio and a full development shop, taking projects from design through to build. That combination suits companies without engineering capacity who need the thing shipped, not just designed. Services: web design and development, mobile and web apps, AI integration, branding. Pricing: project-based. Its real strength: design and build under one contract removes the handoff that causes most timeline slippage. 5. Gravitate Model: studio. Gravitate has operated since 1999 from Main Street in Vancouver, Washington, combining web design with digital marketing. Operating continuously for that long is unusual in a category where agencies appear and disappear quickly. Its marketing orientation means design decisions get argued on performance grounds rather than aesthetic ones. Services: web design and development, SEO and paid media, content, brand. Pricing: project and retainer, quoted. Why it made this list: if the website has a conversion number attached to it, a marketing-led studio beats a pure design studio. 6. Toptal Model: marketplace. Toptal screens freelance designers and developers heavily and connects them to clients directly, positioning on the strength of its vetting rather than the size of its pool. You hire an individual and manage them yourself. That works well when you know exactly what you need and have someone internally able to direct it, and badly when you were hoping the vendor would supply the direction. Services: freelance product designers, UI/UX designers, brand designers, on hourly or full-time arrangements. Pricing: hourly rates vary by designer, typically at the premium end of freelance. Where it beats the alternatives: when you need one senior specialist for a defined stretch rather than a team or a queue. 7. Near Model: marketplace and staffing. Near recruits full-time remote talent in Latin America for US companies, with offices listed in Austin and Sydney. The pitch is time-zone overlap with the United States at a lower cost base than domestic hiring. This is closer to recruitment than to agency work: you get a person who works for you, along with the management responsibility that implies. Services: sourcing and placing full-time remote designers and creative staff, with payroll and compliance handled. Pricing: monthly fee per placement. Why buyers shortlist it: it solves the availability problem without the marketplace churn, provided you actually have someone to manage the hire. 8. DesignCrowd Model: crowdsourced marketplace. DesignCrowd runs design contests where many designers submit concepts against a brief and you pick a winner. It is Australian, with a presence in several markets including the US. The model produces volume of ideas cheaply. It also means most participating designers work for free, and the winning concept arrives without the reasoning behind it, which matters more on brand work than on a one-off graphic. Services: logo design, web design, graphic design, packaging, via contest or direct hire. Pricing: per project, set by you when you post the brief. Where it fits: low-stakes, high-volume needs where seeing thirty directions is worth more than a considered process. 9. Draftss Model: subscription. Draftss offers unlimited graphic design, UI and front-end development on a flat monthly plan, covering a wider technical range than most flat-rate services. Including development in the same subscription is unusual and useful for small teams that would otherwise need a second vendor to implement whatever gets designed. Services: graphic design, UI/UX, front-end development, WordPress and Webflow, illustrations. Pricing: flat monthly plans by number of active requests. Its real strength: design and code from one queue, which suits founders without engineering support. 10. DotYeti Model: subscription. DotYeti provides flat-rate unlimited graphic design with a named designer assigned to the account rather than a rotating pool. Its published business address is on Walker Road in Dover, Delaware, with a distributed creative team. The named-designer detail matters more than it sounds, since brand consistency is the usual casualty of round-robin task assignment. Services: graphic design, brand identity, social and ad creative, presentations, packaging. Pricing: flat monthly tiers by turnaround speed and volume. Why it earns a place here: continuity of designer at a flat-rate price point is a genuinely useful combination. 11. No Limit Creatives Model: subscription. No Limit Creatives runs unlimited graphic and video design from Scalehouse Loop in Bend, Oregon. Video sitting inside the same plan as graphics is the differentiator, since most flat-rate services treat motion as an upsell or exclude it. For marketing teams producing steady social output across both formats, that removes a vendor. Services: graphic design, video editing, motion graphics, social creative, ad variations. Pricing: flat monthly plans, with video included on the higher tiers. Where it fits: social-heavy marketing teams that need volume in both stills and video. 12. Design Buffs Model: subscription. Design Buffs focuses on marketing design for B2B and SaaS teams, leaning on speed and staying on-brand rather than on open-ended creative exploration. The narrower scope is deliberate. A service that only does marketing design for software companies can standardize more of the process than a generalist can. Services: marketing and ad creative, landing pages, ebooks and reports, social, presentation design. Pricing: flat monthly subscription. Why buyers shortlist it: a specialist queue produces more consistent output than a general one, if your needs sit inside its specialism. What outsourced design actually costs The three models are priced on different units, which makes direct comparison harder than it should be. The table converts them to a rough monthly equivalent for a team with steady but not enormous design needs. Route Typical monthly cost What you are really buying Freelancer, ad hoc $2,000 to $8,000 Hours, with management on you Vetted marketplace, part-time $4,000 to $12,000 A senior individual, still managed by you Design subscription $1,490 to $2,995 Output capacity with delivery managed Studio retainer $10,000 to $40,000 Strategy, process and senior direction In-house designer $9,000 to $14,000 loaded A person, plus recruiting and ramp time The in-house row is the one companies underestimate, because the salary is only part of it. Recruiting time, benefits, software licenses, management overhead and the risk that the hire leaves all sit on top, and none of it flexes down in a quiet quarter. Kyivstar's experience is the extreme version of that risk, but a milder form of it applies everywhere: a single in-house designer is a single point of failure. Structuring the team so that outsourced capacity absorbs the peaks is covered in our guide to structuring a design team . How to run an outsourced design team so it works Most outsourcing disappointments trace back to the brief and the contract rather than to the designer. These steps prevent the common ones: Write the brief around the outcome and the constraints, not the deliverable. "A landing page that converts trial signups from paid social" beats "a landing page." Send brand assets, fonts and prior examples with the first task, not after the first draft misses. Agree what a revision round is, in writing, before work starts. Name one internal person who gives feedback. Committee feedback is the single biggest cause of blown timelines. Get a signed copyright assignment covering the deliverables, plus written confirmation of font licensing. Ask for source files at each milestone rather than at the end of the contract. Step five is where the Copyright Office guidance becomes practical rather than theoretical, and step six is what protects you if the relationship ends badly. Neither takes long, and both are far cheaper to do at the start than to litigate later. Continuity deserves its own line in the contract. Interface and UX decisions compound in a way marketing assets do not, so outsourced product design rewards keeping the same designer far more than it rewards the lowest hourly rate. Choosing between the three models Answer one question first: is the hard part deciding what to make, or making it? If it is deciding, buy a studio. ustwo, ParallelHQ, Bilberrry and Gravitate all sell thinking as much as execution, and paying subscription rates for a problem that needed research will produce fast work in the wrong direction. If it is making, buy a subscription or a marketplace hire. The distinction between those two is management capacity. A marketplace gives you a person and expects you to direct them; a subscription gives you output and manages the person for you. Teams without a design lead should be honest that they are buying management as well as design. Our guide to outsourcing graphic design works through that self-assessment in more detail. And whichever you choose, settle ownership before the first file arrives. It is the cheapest insurance in this entire category. If continuous design capacity without a hiring cycle is what you need, that is what our talent model is built around. FAQs What does it cost to outsource design work? It depends on which model you buy. Subscription plans sit between $1,490 and $2,995 monthly, covering continuous output with the delivery managed for you. Vetted marketplace designers typically cost $4,000 to $12,000 a month part-time, though you manage them yourself. Studio retainers start around $10,000 and climb well past $40,000 because you are buying strategy and senior direction alongside production. Compare all three against a loaded in-house cost of roughly $9,000 to $14,000 a month for one designer, which includes benefits, software and recruiting but flexes down for nobody. Do I own the designs if I outsource them? Not automatically, and this catches a lot of buyers. Under US copyright law, work commissioned from a non-employee only counts as work made for hire if it falls within one of nine narrow categories and both parties sign a written agreement saying so. Logos, brand identities, websites and app interfaces are not among those nine categories, so paying the invoice does not by itself transfer copyright. Ask for a signed assignment of copyright covering the specific deliverables, and confirm font licensing separately, since typeface licenses are issued to a named entity and do not transfer with the artwork. Is it better to outsource design overseas or domestically? It depends on what the work demands. Offshore studios and Latin American staffing can reduce cost meaningfully, and time-zone overlap is the variable that decides whether that saving survives contact with reality. Work that needs many short feedback loops, live calls or fast turnarounds suffers most from a large time difference. Work that runs on a clear brief and a weekly review suffers least. Contracting and IP enforcement are also simpler within one jurisdiction, which is worth weighing on brand-critical assets. How do I know if a design subscription will work for my company? Count how many discrete design requests you generated in the last three months. Under roughly four a month, a freelancer is usually cheaper. Above that, and especially if the requests span several formats such as web, social, decks and video, a subscription generally wins because per-project pricing punishes volume while a flat fee does not. The other test is strategic: subscriptions are built for execution, so if your next quarter is dominated by one unresolved positioning question, hire a studio for that piece first. What is the biggest mistake companies make when outsourcing design? Treating the brief as a formality. Deloitte's outsourcing research points at governance and contracting weaknesses, rather than supplier quality, as the reason expected productivity and cost benefits often fail to materialize, and design follows that pattern closely. The specific failures repeat: an outcome never stated, feedback arriving from four people with different opinions, revision limits nobody agreed, and ownership of the files left unresolved until the relationship ends. All four are fixed with paperwork and a named decision-maker before the first task.

title: CACI Selected to Strengthen and Modernize Technology Architectures for U.S. Space Force Guardians
summary: RESTON, Va.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Today CACI International Inc (NYSE: CACI) announced it has been selected to deliver technology that will defend U.S. interests against adversarial threats for the...
body_text: News Releases Download PDF Company Release - 08/17/2026 CACI Selected to Strengthen and Modernize Technology Architectures for U.S. Space Force Guardians RESTON, Va.--( BUSINESS WIRE )--Today CACI International Inc ( NYSE: CACI ) announced it has been selected to deliver technology that will defend U.S. interests against adversarial threats for the U.S. Space Force. Under the National Space Test and Training Complex (NSTTC) Innovative Technology & Engineering – Space Test and Range (NITE‑STAR) contract, CACI will deliver critical technology advancements that strengthen and modernize the test and training architectures required for realistic operations. “This award marks the first of many opportunities to bring together the combined strengths of CACI and ARKA to deliver next-generation space capabilities for the U.S. Space Force,” said Andreas Nonnenmacher, CACI Senior Vice President of Space. “As the space domain becomes increasingly contested, we're equipping Guardians with advanced technologies that enable realistic testing, accelerate mission readiness, and strengthen America's advantage in space.” CACI will collaborate with U.S. Space Force (USSF) OTTI and SYD 81 to rapidly design, develop, and deploy tailored technologies across live, virtual, and constructive (LVC) environments. The development and sustainment of these space and ground‑based capabilities will enhance testing, evaluation, and training operations, ensuring systems are rigorously validated and Guardians are fully prepared for operationally realistic space engagements and advanced threat scenarios. CACI is one of 15 awardees under this multiple award Indefinite Delivery/Indefinite Quantity (IDIQ) valued at up to $981 million over two five-year periods. We deliver advanced technologies that help our customers move faster, operate more efficiently, and anticipate and defeat evolving threats. title: What Sift’s Latest Product Release Changes For Your Team Tomorrow
summary: Explore Sift’s latest fraud prevention product release, including Global Profile Intelligence, fraud attack detection, ATO insights, and workflow automation.
body_text: Product Product News What Sift’s Latest Product Release Changes For Your Team Tomorrow Lots of companies are racing to add “AI-powered” features to their products right now. It’s the trend of the moment, and for some, that’s… Raj Jain Aug 5, 2026 Lots of companies are racing to add “AI-powered” features to their products right now. It’s the trend of the moment, and for some, that’s the whole strategy. When I sit down with actual customers, that’s rarely what they’re asking about. Instead, they ask some version of the same question: what changed in the product this time around that meaningfully impacts what my team can do next week? That question matters more than it sounds. A platform’s job isn’t to ship features. It’s to make sure your team wins, protects revenue, and grows with less friction. Here’s the rundown of our latest release, and why each piece matters more than a changelog usually suggests. See The Whole Customer, Not a Series Of Events The fastest way to make a wrong fraud call is to look at one transaction in isolation. A single event tells you almost nothing about whether the person behind it is trusted or new-and-suspicious. Global Profile Intelligence is our answer to that: near-real-time resolution that keeps network identity links current, plus a new Global Profile widget that puts that context directly where an analyst is already working, inside the Console. We’ve also extended Global Profile criteria into Workflows and Explore, so the routing logic itself can use cross-network context instead of guessing. The point isn’t more data for its own sake. It’s fewer wrong calls and fewer customers caught in the crossfire as a result of incomplete information. Cut Off Attacks At The Root Manual monitoring can’t keep pace with modern fraud attacks. Our new, proactive fraud attack and anomaly detection layer watches for metrics that move outside expected baselines, surfacing alerts with clear investigation paths attached, rather than flagging with no clear next step. It combines adaptive thresholds, historical pattern context, and intelligence shaped by what we’re seeing across the broader network. The difference this makes is time. Catching an attack earlier shifts the odds toward containment instead of cleanup. Detect Account Takeover Earlier & Faster Account takeover prevention lives or dies on how early you can spot a suspicious session and how precisely you can act on it. We’ve strengthened device and login visibility with more persistent iOS Device IDs, deeper advanced intelligence for device and bot-attack detection, and FIBR In-Console benchmarking specifically for account-based risk metrics. None of this adds friction for trusted users, but it does tighten the window on unknown and illegitimate ones. Supercharge Operations Good detection doesn’t matter if the operational layer around it is slow, and every hour your team spends on manual work is an hour not spent stopping fraud. New capabilities like Bulk commenting cuts down repetitive work during investigations. The Workflow Lists API , expanded list scale, and new advanced data export options mean decision logic can be managed programmatically instead of by hand. Even something like our recently-released dark mode is part of the same idea: reduce friction everywhere a fraud team touches the product, beyond the headline features. Context Means Clarity & Confidence In Every Decision None of this is about a single smarter model. Anyone can add generative AI fluff. The real advantage is building actual intelligence on top of it: a decisioning system with actual intelligence that keeps building context, acts on it faster, and gives your team more precise control over the outcome. That’s the throughline behind every release we ship. Today, that shows up as ActivityIQ summarizing session activity in seconds, FIBR In-Console putting your numbers next to the industry’s, ThreatClusters combining customer-specific and global models to cut false positives, and RiskWatch adapting block rates in real time as attacks rise and fall. If you’re already running Sift, this is live in your instance now. If you’re evaluating what a true decisioning platform looks like next to a point solution, this release is a good place to start. Book time with us to see how Sift can change how your business does fraud prevention. Share post on:

title: Aspire Yield, Explained Through Yu'e Bao: A Guide for Chinese-Owned Businesses
summary: If your team has used Yu'e Bao, Aspire Yield will feel familiar. Both let you earn returns on idle balances through low-risk money market funds, with no lock-in and no fixed rate. This guide compares the two side by side — currency exposure (SGD/USD vs. CNY), fund manager structure (Fullerton under Temasek vs. Ant Group's Tianhong), custody protections, liquidity timelines, fees, and how returns are displayed (floating NAV vs. constant NAV) — so Chinese-owned businesses in Singapore can evaluate Aspire Yield with confidence.
body_text: The Core Idea Is the Same Both products solve the same basic problem: money sitting in a transaction account earns nothing, so why not put it to work without locking it away? Yu'e Bao does this by automatically investing your Alipay balance into the Tianhong Yu'ebao Money Market Fund, which holds low-risk instruments like bank deposits, government bonds, and short-term securities. Aspire Yield applies the identical logic to a business account. Idle SGD and USD balances sitting in your Aspire Business Account can be moved into the Fullerton SGD Cash Fund or Fullerton USD Cash Fund — both managed by Fullerton Fund Management, a Singapore-based asset manager under Seviora, which is owned by Temasek (the Singapore government's investment arm). These funds hold short-term, high-quality instruments such as government bills and fixed deposits with approved financial institutions — conceptually the same category of holdings as Yu'e Bao's underlying fund. In other words: this isn't a deposit product, and it isn't a savings account paying a fixed rate. Both are money market fund structures where your capital is invested, not lent to a bank. That distinction matters for both products, and it's worth being upfront about it. Key Differences to Understand Who can use it. Yu'e Bao is built for individual consumers with an Alipay account. Aspire Yield is built exclusively for businesses — specifically, companies incorporated in Singapore that qualify as active Non-Financial Entities. It is not available to individuals, financial institutions, investment companies, or businesses majority-owned by U.S. persons. Currency exposure. Yu'e Bao operates purely in CNY. Aspire Yield lets you hold returns in SGD and USD, which matters if your business already operates internationally and wants to avoid unnecessary FX conversion just to earn a return on cash sitting between transactions. Fund manager, ownership, and oversight. The corporate structure behind each product is worth understanding, because they are quite different in design. With Yu'e Bao, the platform, distributor, and fund manager are essentially one integrated corporate family. Alipay (the platform users interact with) is owned by Ant Group, which in turn holds a 51% controlling stake in Tianhong Asset Management — the company that actually manages the money. Alibaba acquired that stake in October 2013, just months after Yu'e Bao launched, specifically to bring the fund manager inside the group. This vertical integration is what made Yu'e Bao so seamless to use, but it also means a single corporate ecosystem controls the full chain from user interface to asset management. Aspire Yield is structured differently. Aspire is the distributor — the company whose business account you hold and whose app you use. The actual fund management is handled by Fullerton Fund Management, a separately regulated, independently governed asset manager under Seviora, which is owned by Temasek. Aspire does not own Fullerton, and Fullerton does not own Aspire. The two companies operate at arm's length, with Fullerton's mandate being purely to manage the underlying funds according to its own investment discipline and regulatory obligations. This separation means your money is being managed by a dedicated asset manager whose only job is fund management — not a subsidiary built to serve a parent company's platform strategy. The Yield product itself is offered by AFT SG 2 Pte. Ltd., which is regulated by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and holds a Capital Markets Services licence, meaning it operates under Singapore's securities regulatory framework with MAS oversight specifically for dealing in collective investment schemes. Where your money sits. Aspire is explicit that your funds are held in a trust account with a licensed bank, segregated from Aspire's own corporate assets — so in the unlikely event Aspire became insolvent, your money is protected and separate. Similarly, if Fullerton itself ran into trouble, the fund's assets are held by a third-party custodian and shielded from Fullerton's creditors. This segregated custody structure mirrors the protections Chinese investors are familiar with from regulated mutual fund structures, just under Singapore's regulatory regime instead of China's. Liquidity. Yu'e Bao offers same-day access to funds for spending or transfer. Aspire Yield offers same day access for USD if redemption request is submitted before 9am Singapore time and next-business-day access for SGD if redemption request is submitted before 4pm SGT. There's no lock-in period and no minimum investment amount required. Fees. This is one area worth being transparent about. Apart from the fund management fee of 0.16%, Aspire charges an annual fee of 0.5%, accrued daily on your average balance and deducted monthly — you're only charged for days you actually hold funds in the Yield account. Yu'e Bao's costs are baked into the fund's expense ratio rather than charged as a separate visible fee, which comprises management fee (0.3%), sales service fee (0.25%) and custodian fee (0.07%) but conceptually every money market fund carries some layer of management and custodian costs; Aspire's structure is simply more transparent about showing it to you upfront. Returns. Returns on both products move with prevailing interest rates and are not fixed or guaranteed — Yu'e Bao's yield has fallen sharply from its early years as Chinese rates have declined, while Aspire Yield's USD returns currently benefit from the higher US rate environment relative to SGD or CNY. How your returns are shown to you — and one important structural difference. This is worth understanding clearly, because the two products work differently in how they account for returns, and it can look unfamiliar if you're used to Yu'e Bao. Yu'e Bao uses a constant NAV structure. Every unit of the Tianhong Yu'ebao fund is always worth exactly 1 yuan — that number never changes. When the fund earns returns, those returns are credited to you as additional units or accrued interest shown separately in your Alipay balance. You never see the per-unit value drop. This design makes it feel psychologically very close to a savings account: the number you see going in is the same number sitting there every day, and interest shows up as an add-on. Aspire Yield's underlying Fullerton funds use a floating NAV structure — the standard approach for Singapore-regulated unit trusts. The fund's NAV (the price per unit) moves over time. Because Fullerton runs these as accumulating funds, returns are not paid out separately; instead, they are reinvested at the fund level and reflected as a gradually rising NAV. What this means practically: when you invest in Aspire Yield, your units are purchased at the current NAV price, and over time you will see that price rising steadily as the fund earns returns. That upward-trending NAV line is your return — it is not a sign that prices are fluctuating in a risky way. The practical implication for how it feels day to day: with Yu'e Bao, you see a stable number plus interest accruing on top. With Aspire Yield, you see a unit price that trends steadily upward. Both reflect the same underlying reality — low-risk, short-duration investments earning short-term market rates — just displayed differently. Why This Should Feel Familiar, Not Foreign For a Chinese-owned business evaluating Aspire Yield for the first time, the most useful mental model is: this is Yu'e Bao's business-account equivalent, operating under Singapore's regulatory and custody framework instead of China's. The mechanics you already trust — idle balance invested into a low-risk money market fund, no lock-in, daily/near-daily liquidity, returns that move with the market rather than being fixed — all carry over. What changes is the currency, the regulator, the fund manager, and the fact that it's purpose-built for a business account rather than a personal wallet. A Few Things Worth Repeating Plainly Aspire Yield is not a bank deposit and is not covered by deposit insurance. Capital is not guaranteed, and the value of your investment can fluctuate, in the same way it can with Yu'e Bao. Returns are not fixed — they move with market conditions, and past performance never guarantees future returns. Eligibility is limited to qualifying Singapore-incorporated businesses. This article is for general understanding only — it isn't financial, legal, or tax advice. Always check the current rate, fee structure, and terms on Aspire's official pages, or speak with your relationship manager, before making decisions about moving balances into Yield. If anything above raises a question specific to your company's structure or ownership, that's exactly the kind of thing worth raising directly with the Aspire team before opening a Yield account. ‍

title: How to choose a 3PL: Why onboarding matters
summary: Learn how to choose a 3PL by evaluating onboarding, integrations, technology, and scalability. Plus, see how Flowspace makes onboarding seamless.
body_text: TL;DR 3PL onboarding should factor into your decision. It shows how well a provider can get your operation live. A strong onboarding process covers systems, inventory, workflows, testing, and go-live. Evaluate 3PL integrations for both your current channels and future growth. Ask who owns implementation, how transitions are managed, and what support looks like after launch. The right 3PL should make onboarding clear, structured, and scalable. Choosing a 3PL often comes down to cost, warehouse locations, shipping speed, technology, and fulfillment capabilities. But there’s another important factor: how the provider gets you up and running. A strong 3PL onboarding process should make it easier to connect systems, transfer inventory, establish workflows, and launch without disrupting operations. It can also reveal what working with a provider will be like long term. If you’re figuring out how to choose a 3PL, onboarding should be part of the evaluation process. What to consider when choosing a 3PL The right third-party logistics partner (3PL) should fit your current operation and support where your business is headed. Key considerations include: What to consider What to look for Fulfillment capabilities Support for your products, order profiles, shipping requirements, returns, kitting, and special handling needs. Warehouse network Locations that support your customer base, delivery goals, and shipping-cost targets. Technology and visibility Clear visibility into orders, inventory, shipping, and fulfillment performance. Channel support Ability to support ecommerce, marketplaces, wholesale, retail, and future channel expansion. Scalability Capacity to handle seasonal peaks, higher order volume, new products, and geographic growth. Customer support Clear account ownership, escalation paths, and ongoing communication. Pricing and contracts Transparent costs across receiving, storage, fulfillment, shipping, special projects, minimums, and contract terms. These factors tell you what a provider can offer. Onboarding shows you how effectively they can put those capabilities into practice. Why 3PL onboarding should factor into your decision Your relationship with a 3PL starts before the first order ships. During onboarding, the provider needs to understand your operation, connect systems, receive inventory, configure fulfillment rules, document workflows, and prepare for launch. A clear 3PL onboarding process can reduce issues like inaccurate inventory, incorrect shipping rules, integration failures, and unclear responsibilities. It can also be an early indicator of the overall partnership. When choosing a 3PL, ask not only what the provider can do once you’re live, but how they plan to get you there. What does the 3PL onboarding process include? While every provider works differently, onboarding typically includes a few key stages. 1. Discovery and planning The 3PL should understand your products, order volume, sales channels, shipping requirements, packaging, returns, and other operational needs. Both teams should also align on responsibilities, dependencies, and launch timing. 2. Product and SKU setup Product details such as SKUs, dimensions, weights, barcodes, bundles, and handling requirements need to be configured accurately. 3. Systems integration Your commerce and operational systems need to connect with the 3PL so orders, inventory, shipment status, and tracking data can move reliably. 4. Inventory inbounding The provider should establish when and where inventory will arrive, how it should be prepared, and how receiving will be handled. 5. Fulfillment workflows Shipping methods, routing rules, packaging, kitting, inserts, retail requirements, and exception workflows should be documented and configured. 6. Returns Define how returned products will be received, inspected, restocked, or otherwise handled. 7. Testing Test orders should confirm that integrations, inventory data, fulfillment workflows, shipping rules, and tracking are working correctly. 8. Go-live Before launch, inventory should be available, integrations tested, workflows documented, and ownership clear. Where 3PL integrations fit in At a minimum, orders need to reach the fulfillment provider, and shipment information needs to flow back. But modern fulfillment operations often involve much more than a single ecommerce platform and warehouse. Your 3PL integration requirements might include connections to: Ecommerce platforms Marketplaces ERP systems Order management systems Retail and EDI connections Inventory management systems Other logistics and technology partners When evaluating integrations, don't focus solely on your current tech stack. For example, a DTC brand that currently generates most of its orders through its ecommerce website may plan to expand into Amazon, wholesale, or major retail partners. Those channels introduce new fulfillment and inventory requirements. A provider that can support those channels within the same broader fulfillment operation can make expansion easier than one that requires new systems, workflows, or partners every time the business evolves. Inventory visibility is another consideration. As orders come from multiple channels and inventory is distributed across locations, your team needs to know what inventory is available and where. Look for technology that provides centralized inventory visibility and helps your business make decisions around allocation, replenishment, and potential stockouts. Questions to ask about 3PL integrations Which integrations are native, and which require custom development? Who owns the technical implementation? How is order and inventory data synchronized? How are integration errors surfaced and resolved? How will your team know if an order fails to flow correctly? Can the technology support additional sales channels as the business grows? Can you view inventory across multiple fulfillment locations and channels? What inventory management or planning capabilities are available? The goal isn't just to connect two systems, but to create a reliable flow of information across your fulfillment operation. What to ask about onboarding before choosing a 3PL Before signing a contract, ask: What does your 3PL onboarding process look like? How long does onboarding typically take? Who owns implementation? What does your team need from ours? What does the 3PL integration process involve? How will inventory be transferred or received? How are SOPs documented? How do you test workflows before launch? What happens if something delays go-live? What support is available after launch? How would you support a new channel or fulfillment location? The answers should give you a clear sense of timing, ownership, responsibilities, and dependencies. What onboarding with Flowspace looks like With Flowspace, onboarding brings together fulfillment operations, technology, inventory, and launch planning to build a connected fulfillment strategy designed to support growth and scale. Here is a high-level look at what to expect: Understand your fulfillment operation We start by aligning on your products, sales channels, order volume, shipping requirements, customer experience expectations, and other operational needs. It’s also an opportunity to consider what comes next—whether that's higher volume, additional channels, new products, or a broader fulfillment footprint. Connect your commerce ecosystem Our solutions team connects Flowspace with the systems and channels that power your business. While the requirements vary by operation, the goal is the same: remove barriers to great fulfillment. Connecting these systems creates greater visibility across operations while reducing reliance on support tickets, manual workarounds, and rigid workflows. Configure inventory and fulfillment workflows Products, inventory, shipping logic, packaging requirements, returns, and other brand-specific workflows are configured to support the operation. This step translates business requirements into repeatable fulfillment processes before orders begin shipping. Coordinate inventory inbounding Inventory is coordinated into the appropriate fulfillment locations based on the needs of your operation and prepared for launch. A clear inbound plan is especially important for brands transitioning from another 3PL, where inventory needs to move without unnecessarily disrupting customer orders. Test and validate the operation Before launch, orders, inventory data, integrations, routing, and fulfillment workflows are validated to help identify issues before they affect customers. Launch and continue optimizing Go-live isn't the end of fulfillment implementation. As order patterns change and your business grows, fulfillment operations need to evolve with them. Flowspace combines AI-powered fulfillment technology, a flexible nationwide fulfillment network, and hands-on expertise to give brands visibility into operations and the infrastructure to adapt as they scale. Accurate inventory, reliable integrations, clear routing logic, and well-defined workflows create a stronger operational foundation from day one. Choose a partner that can support you from onboarding to scale Choosing a 3PL doesn't stop at capabilities. It's also about how easily a provider can become part of your operation and support future growth. A clear onboarding process, reliable integrations, inventory visibility, and well-defined workflows can reduce disruption at launch and build a stronger foundation for fulfillment. When comparing providers, ask what happens between signing the contract and shipping the first order. The answer can tell you a lot about the partnership ahead. The right 3PL doesn’t just ship orders—it gets you live smoothly and scales with you from day one. Looking for a fulfillment partner that can support your business from onboarding through growth? Learn how Flowspace combines technology, flexible fulfillment infrastructure, and expert support to simplify and scale fulfillment operations. Reach out today . Frequently asked questions about 3PL onboarding What is 3PL onboarding? 3PL onboarding is the process of setting up a brand to begin fulfilling orders with a third-party logistics provider. It typically includes operational planning, product and SKU setup, system integrations, inventory receiving, fulfillment workflow configuration, testing, and preparation for go-live. Why is onboarding important when choosing a partner? Onboarding can provide an early indication of how a 3PL operates. When switching 3PLs , a clear process with defined responsibilities, reliable integrations, thorough testing, and strong communication can help reduce disruption. How long does onboarding take? The timeline depends on the complexity of the operation. Factors such as SKU count, integrations, inventory transfers, sales channels, fulfillment requirements, and custom workflows can all affect how long onboarding takes. Ask prospective providers for a timeline based on your specific operation rather than relying on a standard estimate. What should I look for in a 3PL onboarding process? Look for clear ownership, defined milestones, support for system integrations, a detailed inventory transition plan, documented fulfillment requirements, pre-launch testing, and a clear process for resolving issues before and after go-live. What is a 3PL integration? A 3PL integration connects a fulfillment provider with the systems a brand uses to manage commerce and operations. These may include ecommerce platforms, marketplaces, ERPs, order management systems, retail and EDI connections, and inventory management tools. What integrations should I consider when choosing a 3PL? Consider both the systems you use today and the channels you may add in the future. If you plan to expand from DTC into marketplaces, wholesale, or retail, for example, make sure your 3PL can support those channels and provide visibility into inventory and orders across your operation. What questions should I ask before onboarding? Ask who will own implementation, what information your team needs to provide, how integrations are set up and tested, how inventory will be transferred or received, how fulfillment workflows are documented, and what support is available after launch. How does Flowspace approach onboarding? Flowspace onboarding brings together technology, inventory, fulfillment workflows, and launch planning. The process is designed to connect a brand's commerce ecosystem with its fulfillment operation, establish the workflows needed to fulfill orders, coordinate inventory, validate the operation before launch, and support the business as its needs evolve. ‍

title: Westinghouse and Amentum Partner to Expand Delivery Capacity for APX Fleet Deployment
summary: CHANTILLY, VA., August 4, 2026 – Westinghouse Electric Company and Amentum (NYSE: AMTM), a global leader in advanced engineering and technology solutions,
body_text: Westinghouse and Amentum Partner to Expand Delivery Capacity for APX Fleet Deployment August 4, 2026 • Energy , Engineering & Design , Environmental Solutions , Investors , Partners , Strategic Capabilities Engineering Featured , Press Releases Share CHANTILLY, VA., August 4, 2026 – Westinghouse Electric Company and Amentum (NYSE: AMTM), a global leader in advanced engineering and technology solutions, have entered into a series of agreements supporting the Westinghouse APX technology platform. These agreements augment Westinghouse capabilities to support fleet-scale deployment of its AP1000® reactor while also advancing the development of the AP300™ small modular reactor (SMR). “Westinghouse is pursuing a disciplined APX technology strategy built on the proven AP1000 reactor and extended through the AP300 SMR,” said Dan Sumner, President and Chief Executive Officer of Westinghouse. “We continue to make investments to strengthen our proven APX platform, and our ongoing collaboration with Amentum is expected to accelerate the licensing of the AP300 SMR with the NRC. Separately, our two companies will work together to enhance our engineering and execution capabilities for delivering 1-gigawatt reactors at scale.” “Amentum’s expertise spans the full spectrum of the nuclear project lifecycle, accelerating the development and deployment of advanced nuclear solutions, strengthening energy security and powering the growth of AI and other energy critical industries,” said John Heller, Amentum Chief Executive Officer. “There is an expanding global market for firm baseload power, and our collaboration with Westinghouse will enable us to help meet that demand.” The Westinghouse APX strategy offers a single technology platform enabling the fleet delivery of the AP1000 reactor and the AP300 SMR. The APX platform is based on the proven innovations and technology of the AP1000 plant, including validated engineering, components, licensing strategies, fuel design and supply chain. The APX strategy offers the grid-scale, commercially available AP1000 reactor for near-term global fleet deployments, while developing the AP300 SMR to address additional market segments with smaller energy requirements. Amentum’s engineering capacity and nuclear experience will strengthen the industrial base and delivery model, enabling the repeatable deployment of the APX technology suite. Under the most recent agreement, Westinghouse and Amentum will collaborate to obtain regulatory approval for the AP300 SMR by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, a major milestone in bringing the technology to market. Westinghouse and Amentum have an established history of partnership on nuclear projects worldwide, including nuclear power and decommissioning projects in the United States, United Kingdom, Poland, Slovakia, Lithuania and South Africa. ### About Westinghouse Westinghouse Electric Company is the future of energy, providing reliable, innovative nuclear technologies and services globally. Westinghouse pioneered commercial nuclear power, delivering the world’s first commercial pressurized water reactor in 1957. The company has industrialized more nuclear reactors than any other company, with its technology forming the basis of half of the world’s operating nuclear plants. More than 140 years of innovation makes Westinghouse the preferred partner for advanced technologies covering the complete nuclear energy life cycle. For more information, visit www.westinghousenuclear.com and follow us on Facebook , LinkedIn and X . title: RTX's Raytheon awarded seven-year contract for Tomahawk cruise missiles
summary: Contract accelerates production of critical precision-strike weaponTUCSON, Ariz., Aug. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Raytheon, an RTX (NYSE: RTX) business, will dramatically accelerate the production of Tomahawk cruise missiles for the U.S. Navy over the multi-year period under the terms of an unprecedented $22.9 billion contract, awarded as part of the Department of War's Arsenal of Freedom.This contract follows the landmark agreements between Raytheon and the Department of War and supports the annual production ramp to more than 1,000 Tomahawk missiles and associated support, ensuring a stable, predictable supply for the Navy and allies.
body_text: RTX's Raytheon awarded seven-year contract for Tomahawk cruise missiles August 17, 2026 Share this article on Facebook Share this article on Twitter Share this article on LinkedIn Share this article via email Contract accelerates production of critical precision-strike weapon TUCSON, Ariz. , Aug. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Raytheon, an RTX (NYSE: RTX) business, will dramatically accelerate the production of Tomahawk cruise missiles for the U.S. Navy over the multi-year period under the terms of an unprecedented $22.9 billion contract, awarded as part of the Department of War's Arsenal of Freedom. This contract follows the landmark agreements between Raytheon and the Department of War and supports the annual production ramp to more than 1,000 Tomahawk missiles and associated support, ensuring a stable, predictable supply for the Navy and allies. "Tomahawk is the Navy's most important strike weapon, able to target hostile forces hundreds of miles away without ever risking the lives of our sailors," said Raytheon President Phil Jasper. "We are making significant investments in our workforce, technology, supply chain and facilities to dramatically boost production capacity and meet surging demand." RTX has invested heavily in recent years to ramp production of Tomahawk and other critical munitions, delivering three times more Tomahawks in the first half of 2026 compared to the first half of 2025. With this contract, RTX will increase capacity and collaborate closely with hundreds of small and mid-sized suppliers nationwide to rapidly scale output to meet long-term needs. Tomahawk cruise missiles remain one of the U.S. military's most proven and versatile long range strike capabilities. With a decades‑long record of operational performance, Tomahawk provides military leaders with reliable, flexible options against high value targets from a variety of launch platforms. About Raytheon Raytheon, an RTX business, is a leading provider of defense solutions to help the U.S. government, our allies and partners defend their national sovereignty and ensure their security. For more than 100 years, Raytheon has developed new technologies and enhanced existing capabilities in integrated air and missile defense, smart weapons, missiles, advanced sensors and radars, interceptors, space-based systems, hypersonics and missile defense across land, air, sea and space. About RTX With more than 180,000 global employees, we push the limits of technology and science to redefine how we connect and protect our world. With industry-leading capabilities, we advance aviation, engineer integrated defense systems for operational success, and develop next-generation technology solutions and manufacturing to help global customers address their most critical challenges. The company, with 2025 sales of more than $88 billion, is headquartered in Arlington, Virginia. For questions or to schedule an interview, please contact [email protected] . body_text: Qual curso devo fazer para trabalhar no CRAS? Para ocupar uma vaga de assistente social no CRAS (Centro de Referência de Assistência Social) , é necessário ter graduação em Serviço Social e registro ativo no CRESS. O profissional pode atuar no atendimento e acompanhamento de famílias em situação de vulnerabilidade , na execução de serviços socioassistenciais e em ações de proteção social. No entanto, o CRAS reúne profissionais de diferentes áreas. Dependendo do cargo e das exigências do edital ou da contratação, também podem existir oportunidades para profissionais formados em Psicologia , Pedagogia e outras áreas, além de funções administrativas que podem exigir apenas o ensino médio ou formação específica. title: HF Foods Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results
summary: Net Revenue increased 2.8% to $323.8 million GAAP Net Income increased 413.9% to $2.6 million Adjusted Net Income increased 0.8% to $6.4 million Adjusted EBITDA decreased 2.0% to $13.6 million LAS VEGAS, Aug. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- HF Foods Group Inc.
body_text: HF Foods Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results August 10, 2026 PDF Version Net Revenue increased 2.8% to $323.8 million GAAP Net Income increased 413.9% to $2.6 million Adjusted Net Income increased 0.8% to $6.4 million Adjusted EBITDA decreased 2.0% to $13.6 million LAS VEGAS, Aug. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- HF Foods Group Inc. (NASDAQ: HFFG) (“HF Foods” or the “Company”), a leading distributor of international foodservice solutions to Asian restaurants and other businesses across the United States, today announced results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. (2) Adjusted net income and adjusted earnings per share are based on net income attributable to HF Foods Group Inc. Management Commentary “Our second quarter results reflect continued momentum in a challenging operating environment, marking our sixth consecutive quarter of year-over-year net revenue growth and the highest quarterly revenue in our history," said Felix Lin, President and Chief Executive Officer of HF Foods. "Most significantly, we took a major step in our long-term growth strategy with our agreement to acquire Searay Foods, a leading Canadian importer and distributor of ethnic and specialty seafood. This transaction marks our first expansion outside the United States and extends our proven M&A playbook into a new geography, bringing a margin-accretive business with six proprietary brands into our growing seafood category. M&A remains a core pillar of our growth strategy, and as the strategic acquirer of choice in our space, we will continue to selectively evaluate opportunities that could benefit from our operational expertise and scale. At the same time, with the foundation of our transformation program largely built, we are hyper-focused on executing against the significant organic growth opportunities ahead, including our continued cross-selling initiatives across the Southeast and Midwest. We remain confident in our long-term strategy and our ability to create sustained value for our shareholders as we enhance our position as the leading nationwide Asian specialty food distributor.” Second Quarter 2026 Results Net revenue was $323.8 million for the second quarter of 2026 compared to $314.9 million in the prior year period, an increase of $8.9 million, or 2.8%. The increase was primarily attributable to volume growth and pricing improvement in Seafood and Commodity, partially offset by price decrease in Meat & Poultry. Gross profit was $55.0 million for the quarter, essentially flat compared to $55.1 million in the prior year period. Gross profit margin decreased to 17.0% compared to 17.5% in the prior year period. Margin was impacted by incremental tariffs incurred that took effect beginning Q3 2025, partially offset by the IEEPA tariff refunds received during the quarter. Distribution, selling and administrative expenses increased by $1.2 million, or 2.4%, compared to the prior year period, primarily due to an increase in auto & truck expense reflecting elevated incremental fuel costs together with higher insurance and professional services expense, partially offset by lower personnel expense. Distribution, selling and administrative expenses as a percentage of net revenue decreased to 16.1% compared to 16.2% in the prior year period. Net income increased to $2.6 million compared to a net income of $0.5 million in the prior-year period. The improvement was primarily driven by other income recognized that relate to employee retention credit of $1.8 million, including interest, the IEEPA tariff refund of approximately $1.1 million, and a positive change in fair value of interest rate swap contracts by $1.4 million compared to 2025. These favorable variances were partially offset by $1.3 million decrease in income from operations. Adjusted EBITDA decreased 2.0% to $13.6 million compared to $13.8 million in the prior year period, which was due to various items noted in the Adjusted EBITDA table included in “ Appendix A - Non-GAAP Financial Measures” of this earnings release. Six Months 2026 Results Net revenue was $635.8 million for the six months ended Jun 30, 2026, compared to $613.3 million in the prior year period, an increase of $22.5 million, or 3.7%. The increase was primarily due to volume growth and pricing improvement in Seafood and Commodity, partially offset by price decrease in Meat & Poultry and volume decrease in Asian Specialty. Gross profit slightly decreased by 0.5% to $105.6 million, compared to $106.1 million in the prior year period. Gross profit margin decreased to 16.6% compared to 17.3% in the prior year period. Margin was impacted by incremental tariffs that took effect beginning Q3 2025, partially offset by the IEEPA tariff refunds received during the period. Distribution, selling and administrative expenses increased by $0.9 million, or 0.9% to $101.7 million, compared to the prior year period mainly due to increases in auto & truck and insurance expenses, partially offset by a reduction in personnel and professional services expenses. Distribution, selling and administrative expenses as a percentage of net revenue decreased slightly to 16.0% in 2026 compared to 16.4% in 2025. Net income was $4.0 million compared to net loss of $1.0 million in the prior year period. The improvement was primarily attributable to the recognition of employee retention credit of $1.8 million, including interest, the IEEPA tariff refund of approximately $1.1 million, a gain from the Utah building sale of $1.4 million, and a favorable year-over-year change in fair value of interest rate swap of $3.4 million. These favorable variances were partially offset by a $1.4 million decrease in operating income and a $0.2 million unfavorable change in income taxes. Adjusted EBITDA increased 0.4% to $23.7 million compared to $23.6 million in the prior year period, which was due to various items noted in the Adjusted EBITDA table included in “ Appendix A - Non-GAAP Financial Measures” of this earnings release. Cash Flow and Liquidity Cash provided by operating activities was $14.0 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026, compared to cash provided by operating activities of $10.5 million in the prior year period. Net cash provided by operating activities increased by $3.6 million primarily due to higher income, driven by an increase in other income, and favorable changes in accrued expenses. These favorable impacts were partially offset by lower non-cash expense add-backs. As of June 30, 2026, the Company had cash of $18.1 million, checks issued not presented for payment of $5.6 million and access to approximately $39.7 million in additional funds through the $125.0 million line of credit, subject to a borrowing base calculation. The Company has funded working capital and other capital requirements primarily by cash flow from operations and bank loans, including lines of credit. Cash is required to pay purchase costs for inventory, salaries, fuel and trucking expenses, selling expenses, rental expenses, income taxes, other operating expenses and to service debts. Earnings Call and Webcast HF Foods’ management team will host a live conference call to discuss its financial results today at 1:30 p.m. PT (4:30 p.m. ET). The link to the webcast will be available on the “Events” section of the Company’s Investor Relations website at https://investors.hffoodsgroup.com. Those interested in participating in the live call can dial 1-877-407-0752 or 1-201-389-0912. The webcast will be archived and available for replay. About HF Foods Group Inc. HF Foods Group Inc. is a leading marketer and distributor of fresh produce, frozen and dry food, and non-food products to primarily Asian restaurants and other foodservice customers throughout the United States. HF Foods aims to supply the increasing demand for Asian American restaurant cuisine, leveraging its nationwide network of distribution centers and its strong relations with growers and suppliers of fresh, high-quality specialty restaurant food products and supplies in the US and Asia. Headquartered in Las Vegas, Nevada, HF Foods trades on Nasdaq under the symbol “HFFG”. For more information, please visit www.hffoodsgroup.com.
